metadata.description: Name of the Log Analytics workspace that has Microsoft Sentinel enabled.
Deploy rules enabled. Leave false to tune thresholds and allow-lists first.

properties.displayName: Active Directory reconnaissance (AdFind, SharpHound or several discovery commands)
properties.description:
Before moving laterally, attackers map the domain: trusts, domain controllers, Domain Admins members, and attack
paths. AdFind and SharpHound (BloodHound's collector) fire on their own; built-in commands like nltest and net group
fire when one account runs three or more different kinds within the hour on a device.
Seen in: Conti, BlackCat, Black Basta, Qakbot and Scattered Spider (AdFind and SharpHound feature in many DFIR Report
cases).
Tuning: IT staff run single commands like "net user bob /domain" all day; the three-technique threshold is there for
that reason. Exclude your own BloodHound assessments by device.
Triage: check the account and the parent process. Recon from a user's workstation by a non-IT account, or from a
service account, usually means the device is compromised.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| extend Recon = case(
    FileName =~ "adfind.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "adfind.exe", "AdFind",
    ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)sharphound|invoke-bloodhound|--collectionmethods?\s", "SharpHound",
    FileName =~ "nltest.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/(domain_trusts|dclist|all_trusts|dsgetdc)", "nltest trusts or DCs",
    FileName in~ ("net.exe", "net1.exe") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)group\s+""?(domain admins|enterprise admins|schema admins)", "net group admins",
    FileName in~ ("net.exe", "net1.exe") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(user|group|accounts)\b.*\s/do(m|main)?\b", "net domain query",
    FileName =~ "dsquery.exe", "dsquery",
    ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)get-ad(user|computer|group|domaintrust|trust)\b.*-filter\s+\*", "Get-AD* -Filter *",
    "")
| where isnotempty(Recon)
| summarize Techniques = make_set(Recon), Commands = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DeviceName, AccountName
| where set_has_element(Techniques, "AdFind") or set_has_element(Techniques, "SharpHound") or array_length(Techniques) >= 3

properties.displayName: Same sign-in session used from two countries (possible AiTM token theft)
properties.description:
Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kits proxy the real Microsoft sign-in page, capture the session cookie after
the user completes MFA, and replay it from attacker infrastructure. The stolen session keeps its SessionId, so one
session showing up from two countries within two hours is a strong sign that the cookie is being used somewhere else.
Seen in: Storm-1167 and other AiTM phishing-as-a-service campaigns (EvilProxy, Tycoon 2FA).
Tuning: corporate VPNs and secure web gateways that egress in several countries cause false positives; exclude their
egress IPs. Requires the non-interactive sign-in logs to be connected.
Triage: compare the IPs with the user's usual ones. If one is unfamiliar, revoke sessions (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession),
reset the password, review MFA methods and inbox rules, and look for the phishing email that started it.
properties.query:
union
    (SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(2h) | extend SignInType = "Interactive"),
    (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(2h) | extend SignInType = "NonInteractive")
| where ResultType == "0" and isnotempty(SessionId) and isnotempty(Location)
| summarize Countries = make_set(Location, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10),
    SignInTypes = make_set(SignInType), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName), SessionId
| extend CountryCount = array_length(Countries)
| where CountryCount > 1
| project FirstSeen, LastSeen, UserPrincipalName, SessionId, CountryCount, Countries, IPs, Apps, SignInTypes

properties.displayName: AMSI bypass strings in a command line
properties.description:
The Antimalware Scan Interface lets Defender inspect PowerShell and script content at run time. Attackers disable it
in their own process by flipping amsiInitFailed or patching AmsiScanBuffer before loading their real payload. The
classic bypass strings show up in the command line when it isn't obfuscated further.
Seen in: PowerShell Empire, Cobalt Strike PowerShell stagers and many public loaders.
Tuning: security training labs and red-team exercises; nothing in normal operations.
Triage: look at what ran next in the same PowerShell process (network connections, child processes) and isolate the
device if a payload followed.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)amsiutils|amsiinitfailed|amsiscanbuffer|amsicontext|amsiopensession"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: Burst of anonymous "anyone with the link" sharing links
properties.description:
Anonymous links work for anyone who has the URL, with no sign-in. Creating many of them in an hour is a quiet way to
stage files for exfiltration that doesn't show up as downloads by the account.
Tuning: set the threshold above what your heaviest sharers do in an hour. If anonymous links aren't needed, turn them
off at the tenant level; this rule then catches attempts to re-enable or work around that.
Triage: list the files and sites, check whether the links have been used (AnonymousLinkUsed events), and remove links
the user can't explain.
properties.query:
let threshold = 20;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OfficeWorkload in ("SharePoint", "OneDrive") and Operation == "AnonymousLinkCreated"
| summarize Links = count(), Files = dcount(SourceFileName), SampleFiles = make_set(SourceFileName, 20), Sites = make_set(Site_Url, 10),
    ClientIPs = make_set(ClientIP, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserId
| where Links >= threshold

properties.displayName: Application granted a high-privilege Microsoft Graph application permission
properties.description:
Application permissions (app roles) let an app act on its own, without a user, across the whole tenant. Permissions
such as RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory or AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All are effectively Global Admin, and
full_access_as_app or Mail.ReadWrite read every mailbox. Granting one should always be a reviewed change.
Seen in: Midnight Blizzard's 2024 intrusion at Microsoft (a legacy test app granted full_access_as_app and
RoleManagement rights).
Tuning: approved integrations will appear when first set up; record their app IDs and expect no repeats.
Triage: identify the app, its owner and who granted the permission. If unexpected, remove the app role assignment,
check for new credentials on the app (see the service principal credential hunt) and review its sign-ins.
properties.query:
let PrivilegedAppRoles = dynamic(["RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory", "AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All",
    "Application.ReadWrite.All", "Directory.ReadWrite.All", "Domain.ReadWrite.All", "Policy.ReadWrite.ConditionalAccess",
    "PrivilegedAccess.ReadWrite.AzureADGroup", "User.ReadWrite.All", "Group.ReadWrite.All", "Mail.ReadWrite",
    "Mail.Send", "Mail.Read", "full_access_as_app", "Files.ReadWrite.All", "Sites.FullControl.All", "Sites.ReadWrite.All"]);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationName == "Add app role assignment to service principal" and Result =~ "success"
| mv-apply Prop = TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties on (
    summarize Props = make_bag(bag_pack(tostring(Prop.displayName), trim(@'"', tostring(Prop.newValue))))
  )
| extend AppRole = tostring(Props["AppRole.Value"]), ClientApp = tostring(Props["ServicePrincipal.DisplayName"]),
    ClientAppId = tostring(Props["ServicePrincipal.AppId"]),
    Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| where AppRole in (PrivilegedAppRoles)
| project TimeGenerated, ClientApp, ClientAppId, AppRole, ResourceApp = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName), Actor, ActorIP

properties.displayName: New owner added to an application or service principal
properties.description:
Owners of an app registration or service principal can add client secrets and certificates to it, then sign in as
the app with all of its permissions. Adding an owner is a low-visibility way to take over a privileged app.
Tuning: developer teams add owners during normal work; consider scoping to apps with high-privilege permissions by
adding a watchlist of app IDs, and skip the alert when the actor adds themselves to an app they created that day.
Triage: check whether the new owner works on that app and whether new credentials were added to it afterwards.
properties.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationName in ("Add owner to application", "Add owner to service principal") and Result =~ "success"
| extend NewOwner = coalesce(tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName), tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)),
    App = tostring(TargetResources[1].displayName), AppObjectId = tostring(TargetResources[1].id),
    Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, App, AppObjectId, NewOwner, Actor, ActorIP

properties.displayName: Burst of AccessDenied errors across many AWS APIs from one identity
properties.description:
When attackers get a new set of AWS keys, they don't know what the keys can do, so they try a wide range of List,
Describe and Get calls and collect the failures. Twenty-five or more access-denied errors across ten or more APIs in
an hour is that pattern; a broken app usually fails the same one or two calls over and over.
Seen in: Pacu, ScoutSuite-style enumeration with stolen keys, and the "enumerate-iam" approach seen in cloud
credential-theft campaigns.
Tuning: CSPM and security scanners with deliberately narrow permissions can do this; exclude their role ARNs.
Triage: find where the key came from (leaked in code? an instance profile?), check the source IP and user agent, and
deactivate or rotate the credentials if the activity isn't yours.
properties.query:
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ErrorCode in ("AccessDenied", "AccessDeniedException", "UnauthorizedOperation", "Client.UnauthorizedOperation", "UnauthorizedAccess")
| summarize Errors = count(), DistinctApis = dcount(EventName), Apis = make_set(EventName, 30), Services = make_set(EventSource, 20),
    IPs = make_set(SourceIpAddress, 10), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by UserIdentityArn, RecipientAccountId
| where Errors >= 25 and DistinctApis >= 10

properties.displayName: AWS access key created for a different IAM user
properties.description:
Creating an access key for another user gives the caller a second, long-lived identity that keeps working after their
own credentials are revoked. Attackers with iam:CreateAccessKey do this to persist and to blend in as a service user.
Tuning: identity teams provisioning keys for service users will appear; prefer roles over keys, and allow-list the
provisioning role if needed.
Triage: check whether the target user needed a new key, deactivate it if not, and review the caller's other IAM
changes in the same session.
properties.query:
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventName == "CreateAccessKey" and isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend TargetUser = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).userName),
    CallerName = iff(isnotempty(UserIdentityUserName), UserIdentityUserName, extract(@"[^/]+$", 0, UserIdentityArn))
| where isnotempty(TargetUser) and TargetUser != CallerName
| project TimeGenerated, UserIdentityArn, CallerName, TargetUser, SourceIpAddress, RecipientAccountId, UserAgent

properties.displayName: AWS administrator-level policy attached or written
properties.description:
Attaching the AdministratorAccess managed policy, or writing an inline or custom policy that allows "*" on "*",
turns a limited identity into a full admin. This is the most common privilege-escalation end state in AWS.
Seen in: Pacu and Stratus Red Team privilege-escalation modules, and many AWS incident write-ups.
Tuning: account bootstrapping and break-glass roles are expected; scope them out by role name. Prefer IAM Identity
Center permission sets so direct attachments are rare enough to review each one.
Triage: identify the target user, role or group and who made the change, detach the policy if it isn't approved, and
review the target's activity since.
properties.query:
let Managed = AWSCloudTrail
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where EventName in ("AttachUserPolicy", "AttachRolePolicy", "AttachGroupPolicy") and isempty(ErrorCode)
    | where RequestParameters contains "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess"
    | extend Grant = "AdministratorAccess managed policy";
let Inline = AWSCloudTrail
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where EventName in ("PutUserPolicy", "PutRolePolicy", "PutGroupPolicy", "CreatePolicy", "CreatePolicyVersion") and isempty(ErrorCode)
    | extend Doc = parse_json(tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).policyDocument))
    | mv-expand Statement = iff(gettype(Doc.Statement) == "array", Doc.Statement, pack_array(Doc.Statement))
    | where tostring(Statement.Effect) == "Allow"
    | where tostring(Statement.Action) == "*" or tostring(Statement.Action) contains '"*"'
    | where tostring(Statement.Resource) == "*" or tostring(Statement.Resource) contains '"*"'
    | extend Grant = "Policy allowing * on *"
    | project-away Doc, Statement;
union Managed, Inline
| extend P = parse_json(RequestParameters)
| extend Target = coalesce(tostring(P.userName), tostring(P.roleName), tostring(P.groupName), tostring(P.policyName), tostring(P.policyArn))
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by EventName, Grant, Target, UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress, RecipientAccountId

properties.displayName: AWS console sign-in by an IAM user without MFA
properties.description:
A successful console sign-in by an IAM user (or root) with no MFA means a password alone opened the console. Stolen
IAM passwords are common in infostealer logs.
Tuning: users who sign in through IAM Identity Center or a federated IdP appear as assumed roles and are excluded.
The fix for repeat offenders is an IAM policy that denies everything without aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent.
Triage: confirm with the user, enforce MFA on the account, and review the session's API calls.
properties.query:
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventName == "ConsoleLogin" and ResponseElements contains '"ConsoleLogin":"Success"'
| where UserIdentityType in ("IAMUser", "Root")
| where AdditionalEventData contains '"MFAUsed":"No"'
| extend User = iff(isnotempty(UserIdentityUserName), UserIdentityUserName, UserIdentityArn)
| project TimeGenerated, User, UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress, UserAgent, RecipientAccountId

properties.displayName: New IAM user created and given credentials in the same session
properties.description:
Creating an IAM user and then immediately giving it a console password or access key is a classic persistence move:
a backdoor account that survives rotation of the attacker's original credentials. Most organizations that use IAM
Identity Center should rarely create IAM users at all.
Tuning: if Terraform or CloudFormation creates IAM users, exclude the pipeline role ARN.
Triage: check who asked for the user, delete it (and its keys) if no one did, and review the creator's activity.
properties.query:
let Created = AWSCloudTrail
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where EventName == "CreateUser" and isempty(ErrorCode)
    | extend NewUser = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).userName)
    | project CreatedAt = TimeGenerated, NewUser, Creator = UserIdentityArn, CreatorIP = SourceIpAddress, RecipientAccountId;
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventName in ("CreateLoginProfile", "CreateAccessKey", "AttachUserPolicy", "AddUserToGroup", "PutUserPolicy") and isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend NewUser = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).userName)
| join kind=inner Created on NewUser, RecipientAccountId
| where TimeGenerated >= CreatedAt
| summarize FollowUps = make_set(EventName), LastChange = max(TimeGenerated) by NewUser, Creator, CreatorIP, RecipientAccountId, CreatedAt
| where set_has_element(FollowUps, "CreateLoginProfile") or set_has_element(FollowUps, "CreateAccessKey")

properties.displayName: AWS KMS key disabled or scheduled for deletion
properties.description:
Data encrypted with a deleted KMS key is gone for good. Attackers schedule key deletion (or disable keys) to destroy
data or hold it to ransom, sometimes after re-encrypting data with a key they control.
Tuning: key rotation projects and decommissioning disable or delete keys occasionally; match them to a ticket.
Triage: cancel the deletion (CancelKeyDeletion) or re-enable the key straight away; the 7-30 day waiting period is
your window. Then investigate the caller.
properties.query:
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventSource == "kms.amazonaws.com" and EventName in ("ScheduleKeyDeletion", "DisableKey") and isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend KeyId = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).keyId),
    PendingDays = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).pendingWindowInDays)
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, KeyId, PendingDays, UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress, RecipientAccountId, AWSRegion

properties.displayName: AWS CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config or flow logs disabled
properties.description:
Stopping or deleting a trail, turning off GuardDuty, or removing Config recorders and VPC flow logs removes the
evidence and the alerts for whatever comes next. It's one of the first things attackers do with stolen admin keys.
Seen in: most documented AWS intrusions (for example the cryptomining and data-theft campaigns reported by AWS and
Datadog); a standard step in Stratus Red Team and Pacu.
Tuning: UpdateTrail and PutEventSelectors are also used for routine changes; review the request parameters before
closing. Use an SCP to deny these calls outside a break-glass role.
Triage: turn the service back on, find out how the caller got its credentials, and check what it did right after.
properties.query:
let TamperEvents = dynamic(["StopLogging", "DeleteTrail", "UpdateTrail", "PutEventSelectors", "DeleteDetector",
    "DisassociateFromAdministratorAccount", "DisassociateFromMasterAccount", "StopMonitoringMembers", "DeleteMembers",
    "DeleteFlowLogs", "DeleteConfigurationRecorder", "StopConfigurationRecorder", "DeleteDeliveryChannel", "DisableSecurityHub"]);
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| where EventName in (TamperEvents) or (EventName == "UpdateDetector" and RequestParameters contains '"enable":false')
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), EventNames = make_set(EventName), Regions = make_set(AWSRegion), Requests = make_set(RequestParameters, 5)
    by UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress, RecipientAccountId

properties.displayName: AWS root user activity
properties.description:
The root user can't be limited by IAM policies or SCPs and should be locked away with hardware MFA. Any activity by
root, other than the handful of tasks that require it, needs explaining.
Tuning: AWS service events performed on root's behalf are excluded. Expect a few events when someone does a
root-only task (changing the support plan, closing the account); match them to a ticket.
Triage: confirm who holds the root credentials and whether they signed in. If not, change the root password, replace
its MFA device and review every API call in the session.
properties.query:
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where UserIdentityType == "Root" and EventTypeName != "AwsServiceEvent"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Events = count(), EventNames = make_set(EventName, 30), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5)
    by RecipientAccountId, SourceIpAddress

properties.displayName: S3 bucket made public or its public access block removed
properties.description:
A bucket policy with Principal "*", a public ACL, or removing Block Public Access exposes the bucket's contents to
the internet. Attackers do this to pull data out without their own credentials showing up in data-access logs;
more often it's a mistake that leads to a breach.
Tuning: buckets that host public websites or downloads are expected; list them in PublicBuckets.
Triage: re-enable Block Public Access, check S3 server access logs or CloudTrail data events for anonymous GETs while
the bucket was open, and review who made the change.
properties.query:
let PublicBuckets = dynamic(["www.contoso.example"]);
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventSource == "s3.amazonaws.com" and isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend Bucket = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).bucketName)
| where Bucket !in (PublicBuckets)
| extend Change = case(
    EventName == "PutBucketAcl" and RequestParameters matches regex @"(?i)AllUsers|AuthenticatedUsers|public-read", "Public ACL",
    EventName == "PutBucketPolicy" and RequestParameters matches regex @"""Principal""\s*:\s*(""\*""|\{\s*""AWS""\s*:\s*""\*""\s*\})"
        and RequestParameters contains '"Allow"', "Public bucket policy",
    EventName in ("DeleteBucketPublicAccessBlock", "DeleteAccountPublicAccessBlock"), "Public access block deleted",
    EventName in ("PutBucketPublicAccessBlock", "PutAccountPublicAccessBlock")
        and RequestParameters matches regex @"""(BlockPublicAcls|IgnorePublicAcls|BlockPublicPolicy|RestrictPublicBuckets)""\s*:\s*false", "Public access block weakened",
    "")
| where isnotempty(Change)
| project TimeGenerated, Bucket, Change, EventName, UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress, RecipientAccountId, RequestParameters

properties.displayName: Many AWS secrets retrieved by one identity
properties.description:
Reading 20 or more different secrets (Secrets Manager, or SSM parameters with decryption) in an hour is credential
harvesting: one compromised identity collecting database passwords, API keys and tokens for the next step. Apps read
the same few secrets repeatedly; people and attackers read many different ones.
Tuning: deployment pipelines that inject many secrets at release time will appear; exclude their role ARNs.
Triage: list the secrets read, rotate them, and work out how the caller obtained its credentials.
properties.query:
let threshold = 20;
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| where EventName in ("GetSecretValue", "BatchGetSecretValue")
    or (EventName in ("GetParameter", "GetParameters", "GetParametersByPath") and RequestParameters contains '"withDecryption":true')
| extend P = parse_json(RequestParameters)
| extend Secret = coalesce(tostring(P.secretId), tostring(P.name), tostring(P.names), tostring(P.path), tostring(P.secretIdList))
| summarize Requests = count(), Secrets = dcount(Secret), SampleSecrets = make_set(Secret, 20), IPs = make_set(SourceIpAddress, 10),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by UserIdentityArn, RecipientAccountId
| where Secrets >= threshold

properties.displayName: EBS, AMI or RDS snapshot shared with another account or made public
properties.description:
Sharing a disk, image or database snapshot with an outside AWS account is a fast way to copy entire volumes or
databases out, and it doesn't create any data-transfer events in your account. Making a snapshot public exposes it to
everyone.
Seen in: documented AWS data-theft cases and Stratus Red Team's exfiltration techniques.
Tuning: list your own organization's account IDs in TrustedAccounts (backup and DR accounts in particular).
Triage: remove the share (modify the attribute with "remove"), check whether the other account copied it (you can't
see that directly; assume yes), and find out how the caller got permission.
properties.query:
let TrustedAccounts = dynamic(["111111111111"]);
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventName in ("ModifySnapshotAttribute", "ModifyImageAttribute", "ModifyDBSnapshotAttribute", "ModifyDBClusterSnapshotAttribute")
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend P = parse_json(RequestParameters)
| extend AddList = case(
    EventName == "ModifySnapshotAttribute", P.createVolumePermission.add.items,
    EventName == "ModifyImageAttribute", P.launchPermission.add.items,
    P.valuesToAdd)
| mv-expand Item = AddList
| extend SharedWith = iff(gettype(Item) == "dictionary", coalesce(tostring(Item.userId), tostring(Item.group)), tostring(Item))
| where isnotempty(SharedWith)
| where SharedWith =~ "all" or (SharedWith != RecipientAccountId and SharedWith !in (TrustedAccounts))
| extend Resource = coalesce(tostring(P.snapshotId), tostring(P.imageId), tostring(P.dBSnapshotIdentifier), tostring(P.dBClusterSnapshotIdentifier)),
    Public = SharedWith =~ "all"
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, Resource, SharedWith, Public, UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress, RecipientAccountId

properties.displayName: Azure backup protection removed or backup vault deleted
properties.description:
Ransomware crews delete or disable backups before encrypting so the victim can't restore. In Azure that means
stopping protection on backed-up items, changing a vault's soft-delete or immutability settings, or deleting vaults.
Seen in: Storm-0501 cloud ransomware (2024-2025), which deleted Azure backups before mass deletion and encryption.
Tuning: decommissioning a VM stops its protection; those changes should match a change ticket.
Triage: check soft-deleted backup items (they can be restored for 14 days by default), lock the vault with
immutability and multi-user authorization, and investigate the caller.
properties.query:
let BackupOps = dynamic(["MICROSOFT.RECOVERYSERVICES/VAULTS/DELETE",
    "MICROSOFT.RECOVERYSERVICES/VAULTS/BACKUPFABRICS/PROTECTIONCONTAINERS/PROTECTEDITEMS/DELETE",
    "MICROSOFT.RECOVERYSERVICES/VAULTS/BACKUPCONFIG/WRITE", "MICROSOFT.RECOVERYSERVICES/VAULTS/BACKUPPOLICIES/DELETE",
    "MICROSOFT.DATAPROTECTION/BACKUPVAULTS/DELETE", "MICROSOFT.DATAPROTECTION/BACKUPVAULTS/BACKUPINSTANCES/DELETE",
    "MICROSOFT.DATAPROTECTION/BACKUPVAULTS/BACKUPPOLICIES/DELETE"]);
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationNameValue in~ (BackupOps) and ActivityStatusValue in~ ("Success", "Succeeded")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Operations = make_set(OperationNameValue), Resources = make_set(_ResourceId, 20),
    Count = count() by Caller, CallerIpAddress, SubscriptionId

properties.displayName: Global Administrator elevated access to all Azure subscriptions
properties.description:
The "Access management for Azure resources" toggle gives a Global Administrator User Access Administrator at the root
scope, and with it control over every subscription and management group. It's a well-known jump from Entra ID to
Azure and should be used only briefly in emergencies.
Seen in: Storm-0501 (2024) and other Entra-to-Azure pivots after a Global Admin compromise.
Tuning: none expected; every use should match an emergency change.
Triage: confirm with the admin. Make sure the elevation was removed afterwards (the root-scope assignment should be
gone) and review Azure activity by that account since the elevation.
properties.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationName == "User has elevated their access to User Access Administrator for their Azure Resources"
| extend Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, ActorIP, Result, Category

properties.displayName: Azure diagnostic settings, Log Analytics workspace or Sentinel rules deleted
properties.description:
Deleting diagnostic settings stops logs flowing to Sentinel; deleting the workspace, analytics rules or data
connectors removes detection itself. Attackers who reach Azure control-plane rights do this before the noisy part.
Seen in: Storm-0501 and other cloud ransomware operators; a standard step in CISA's cloud defense-evasion guidance.
Tuning: infrastructure-as-code pipelines that recreate settings will appear; exclude their service principals by
object ID after confirming they only run from your pipeline.
Triage: restore the setting or rule, identify the caller and IP, and review the caller's other Azure activity in the
same hour.
properties.query:
let TamperOps = dynamic(["MICROSOFT.INSIGHTS/DIAGNOSTICSETTINGS/DELETE", "MICROSOFT.OPERATIONALINSIGHTS/WORKSPACES/DELETE",
    "MICROSOFT.OPERATIONALINSIGHTS/WORKSPACES/DATASOURCES/DELETE", "MICROSOFT.OPERATIONALINSIGHTS/WORKSPACES/DATACOLLECTIONRULES/DELETE",
    "MICROSOFT.INSIGHTS/DATACOLLECTIONRULES/DELETE", "MICROSOFT.INSIGHTS/DATACOLLECTIONRULEASSOCIATIONS/DELETE",
    "MICROSOFT.SECURITYINSIGHTS/ALERTRULES/DELETE", "MICROSOFT.SECURITYINSIGHTS/DATACONNECTORS/DELETE",
    "MICROSOFT.SECURITYINSIGHTS/AUTOMATIONRULES/DELETE"]);
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationNameValue in~ (TamperOps) and ActivityStatusValue in~ ("Success", "Succeeded")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Operations = make_set(OperationNameValue), Resources = make_set(_ResourceId, 20)
    by Caller, CallerIpAddress, SubscriptionId

properties.displayName: Mass deletion of Azure resources by one caller
properties.description:
Twenty-five or more distinct resources deleted by one caller in an hour. Destructive attacks in the cloud often skip
encryption and just delete storage accounts, VMs, disks and databases after taking the data.
Seen in: Storm-0501 (mass deletion after exfiltration), and the 2022 Lapsus$ intrusions.
Tuning: environment teardown pipelines delete in bulk; exclude their service principal IDs or the dev subscription.
Triage: identify the caller, stop further damage (remove their role assignments, disable the account), then check
resource locks, soft delete and backups for recovery.
properties.query:
let threshold = 25;
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationNameValue endswith "/DELETE" and ActivityStatusValue in~ ("Success", "Succeeded")
| summarize Deleted = dcount(_ResourceId), ResourceTypes = make_set(tolower(OperationNameValue), 20), Sample = make_set(_ResourceId, 20),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Caller, CallerIpAddress
| where Deleted >= threshold

properties.displayName: Owner or User Access Administrator assigned in Azure RBAC
properties.description:
Owner, User Access Administrator and Role Based Access Control Administrator can grant any access, so an assignment
of one of them is a privilege-escalation or persistence step unless it was planned. This catches assignments made
directly in Azure RBAC, which the Entra role rules don't see.
Tuning: if you use PIM for Azure resources, activations also write role assignments; exclude the PIM service caller
(it appears as an MS-PIM principal) or alert only on assignments at subscription or management-group scope.
Triage: check the principal that received the role (a new guest or service principal is the worst case), the scope,
and who assigned it. Remove it if it isn't tied to a change.
properties.query:
let PrivilegedRoles = datatable(RoleId: string, RoleName: string) [
    "8e3af657-a8ff-443c-a75c-2fe8c4bcb635", "Owner",
    "18d7d88d-d35e-4fb5-a5c3-7773c20a72d9", "User Access Administrator",
    "f58310d9-a9f6-439a-9e8d-f62e7b41a168", "Role Based Access Control Administrator"
];
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationNameValue =~ "MICROSOFT.AUTHORIZATION/ROLEASSIGNMENTS/WRITE"
| where ActivityStatusValue !in~ ("Failure", "Failed")
| extend Body = tostring(Properties_d)
| extend RoleId = tolower(extract(@"roleDefinitions/([0-9a-fA-F\-]{36})", 1, Body)),
    PrincipalId = extract(@"(?i)principalId\\?""?\s*:\s*\\?""([0-9a-fA-F\-]{36})", 1, Body),
    PrincipalType = extract(@"(?i)principalType\\?""?\s*:\s*\\?""(\w+)", 1, Body)
| join kind=inner PrivilegedRoles on RoleId
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), PrincipalId = take_any(PrincipalId), PrincipalType = take_any(PrincipalType)
    by Caller, CallerIpAddress, RoleName, Scope = _ResourceId
| extend AtSubscriptionOrAbove = Scope !contains "/resourcegroups/"

properties.displayName: VM Run Command used by an account that hasn't used it before
properties.description:
Run Command executes scripts as SYSTEM or root on any VM the caller can manage, with no network access to the VM
needed. Attackers with Azure Contributor rights use it to push ransomware or tooling to servers. This rule flags
callers with no Run Command activity in the previous 14 days.
Seen in: Storm-0501, Octo Tempest, and red-team guidance on Azure lateral movement.
Tuning: break-glass and automation identities may use it rarely; once confirmed, they won't fire again for 14 days.
Triage: get the script content (the Run Command history on the VM, or Get-AzVMRunCommand), check who ran it and from
where, and look at the VM for new processes or files right after.
properties.query:
let RunCommandOps = dynamic(["MICROSOFT.COMPUTE/VIRTUALMACHINES/RUNCOMMAND/ACTION", "MICROSOFT.COMPUTE/VIRTUALMACHINES/RUNCOMMANDS/WRITE",
    "MICROSOFT.COMPUTE/VIRTUALMACHINESCALESETS/VIRTUALMACHINES/RUNCOMMAND/ACTION", "MICROSOFT.HYBRIDCOMPUTE/MACHINES/RUNCOMMANDS/WRITE"]);
let KnownCallers = AzureActivity
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. ago(1h))
    | where OperationNameValue in~ (RunCommandOps)
    | distinct Caller;
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationNameValue in~ (RunCommandOps) and ActivityStatusValue !in~ ("Failure", "Failed")
| where Caller !in (KnownCallers)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), VMs = make_set(_ResourceId, 20), VMCount = dcount(_ResourceId)
    by Caller, CallerIpAddress, SubscriptionId

properties.displayName: Break-glass account sign-in attempt
properties.description:
Emergency-access ("break-glass") accounts exist for when normal admin access fails. They should almost never be used,
so any sign-in attempt, successful or not, needs an immediate human look.
Tuning: replace the BreakGlassAccounts list with your accounts, or with a Sentinel watchlist
(_GetWatchlist('BreakGlassAccounts') | project SearchKey). Expected volume is near zero; every alert is worth a call.
Triage: Call the account's custodians straight away. If no one used it, reset the password, check the sign-in's IP and
device, and review every action taken in the session.
properties.query:
let BreakGlassAccounts = dynamic(["breakglass1@contoso.com", "breakglass2@contoso.com"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(15m)
| where UserPrincipalName in~ (BreakGlassAccounts)
| extend Outcome = iff(ResultType == "0", "Success", "Failure")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, Outcome, ResultType, ResultDescription, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, UserAgent

properties.displayName: Repeated failed passwords then a successful sign-in from the same IP
properties.description:
Ten or more wrong-password or lockout failures for one user from one IP, followed by a success from that same IP, is
the shape of a guessing attack that worked.
Tuning: a user fighting a stale saved password on their own device can trigger this; the IP usually gives it away (a
home ISP the user has used before vs. a hosting provider).
Triage: check whether the IP is one the user has used before. If not, reset the password, revoke sessions, and check
what the session did.
properties.query:
let FailureCodes = dynamic(["50126", "50053"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| extend UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName)
| summarize Failures = countif(ResultType in (FailureCodes)), FirstFailure = minif(TimeGenerated, ResultType in (FailureCodes)),
    Successes = countif(ResultType == "0"), LastSuccess = maxif(TimeGenerated, ResultType == "0"),
    Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), Location = take_any(Location)
    by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| where Failures >= 10 and Successes > 0 and LastSuccess > FirstFailure

properties.displayName: Conditional Access policy deleted or disabled
properties.description:
Conditional Access enforces MFA and device rules. Deleting a policy, or switching it from enforced to off or
report-only, removes a control at once and is a known step in tenant takeover.
Tuning: changes should go through change management; correlate alerts with approved change tickets.
Triage: Re-enable or restore the policy, confirm the change with the actor, and review sign-ins that the policy would have
blocked while it was off.
properties.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationName in ("Delete conditional access policy", "Update conditional access policy") and Result =~ "success"
| extend PolicyName = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName),
    NewValue = tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties[0].newValue),
    OldValue = tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties[0].oldValue)
| extend NewState = extract(@'"state"\s*:\s*"(\w+)"', 1, NewValue), OldState = extract(@'"state"\s*:\s*"(\w+)"', 1, OldValue)
| where OperationName == "Delete conditional access policy"
    or (OldState == "enabled" and NewState in ("disabled", "enabledForReportingButNotEnforced"))
| extend Change = iff(OperationName startswith "Delete", "Deleted", strcat(OldState, " -> ", NewState)),
    Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| project TimeGenerated, PolicyName, Change, Actor, ActorIP

properties.displayName: Cross-tenant access or sync settings changed
properties.description:
Cross-tenant access settings decide which outside tenants can sign in to yours, and whether their MFA and device
claims are trusted. Cross-tenant sync can push users from another tenant into yours. An attacker who adds their own
tenant as a trusted partner gets a quiet way back in.
Seen in: Microsoft's guidance on cross-tenant synchronization abuse for lateral movement and persistence.
Tuning: changes should be rare and tied to a known B2B partner project.
Triage: check which partner tenant ID was added or changed and whether inbound trust or sync was turned on. Revert
anything you can't tie to a known partner.
properties.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationName contains "cross-tenant" and Result =~ "success"
| where OperationName !startswith "Get " and OperationName !startswith "List "
| extend Target = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName), TargetId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id),
    Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress),
    NewValue = tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties[0].newValue)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Target, TargetId, Actor, ActorIP, NewValue

properties.displayName: Cryptocurrency miner started
properties.description:
Attackers who get into cloud VMs, containers or exposed servers often just mine cryptocurrency. Miners are easy to
spot by name (XMRig and friends) or by their pool arguments (stratum+tcp://, --donate-level, RandomX algorithms).
Seen in: TeamTNT, Kinsing, 8220 Gang and opportunistic exploitation of exposed Docker, Redis and Kubernetes.
Tuning: none expected on business systems.
Triage: kill the process, find how it got there (cron, systemd unit, container image, exploited service), and treat
the host as compromised: miners are often a sign of wider access.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^(xmrig|xmr-stak|minerd|cpuminer|nbminer|t-rex|lolminer|phoenixminer|kdevtmpfsi|kinsing)(\.exe)?$"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)stratum\+(tcp|ssl|tls)://|--donate-level|--coin[= ]+(monero|xmr)\b|--algo[= ]+(rx/0|randomx|cryptonight)"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

properties.displayName: Cloud sync tool used to copy data out (rclone, MEGA, restic)
properties.description:
Ransomware crews steal data before encrypting, and rclone (often renamed to look like a system file) is their
favorite tool, with MEGA, restic and similar close behind. This catches rclone by name, by its original file name
when renamed, and by its distinctive flags.
Seen in: Conti, BlackCat, LockBit, Royal and Scattered Spider data theft (CISA #StopRansomware advisories).
Tuning: if IT uses rclone for migrations, allow-list the specific device and account rather than the tool.
Triage: identify the remote (the "name:" before the path, and the rclone.conf file), estimate what was copied, block
the destination, and treat it as a likely ransomware precursor: hunt for credential dumping and backup deletion.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| extend IsRclone = FileName in~ ("rclone.exe", "rclone") or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "rclone.exe"
| where (IsRclone and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s(copy|sync|move|copyto|moveto)\s")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s(copy|sync)\s.*\s[\w\-]+:\S*.*--(transfers|multi-thread-streams|no-check-certificate|ignore-existing|max-age)"
    or FileName in~ ("megacmd.exe", "megacmdserver.exe", "mega-put.exe", "megasync.exe", "restic.exe", "restic")
| extend Renamed = IsRclone and FileName !in~ ("rclone.exe", "rclone")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, Renamed, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName

properties.displayName: Directory replication requested by an account that isn't a domain controller (DCSync)
properties.description:
DCSync impersonates a domain controller and asks a real DC to replicate password data, giving the attacker every hash
in the domain (including krbtgt) without touching NTDS.dit. Only domain controllers, and the Entra Connect sync
account if you use password hash sync, should ever make these requests.
Seen in: Mimikatz lsadump::dcsync and Impacket secretsdump, used in most domain-wide compromises.
Tuning: requires "Audit Directory Service Access" with a SACL on the domain object. Machine accounts ending in $ are
excluded (domain controllers); the Entra Connect AD DS connector account (MSOL_*) is excluded, so add yours if it's
named differently.
Triage: treat as full domain compromise: identify the account and source host, then plan a krbtgt double reset and
privileged credential rotation.
properties.query:
let ReplicationRights = dynamic(["1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2", "1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2",
    "89e95b76-444d-4c62-991a-0facbeda640c"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID == 4662 and AccessMask == "0x100"
| extend Guids = extract_all(@"([0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12})", tolower(Properties))
| where array_length(set_intersect(Guids, ReplicationRights)) > 0
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$" and SubjectUserName !startswith "MSOL_"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Requests = count(), DomainControllers = make_set(Computer, 5) by SubjectUserName, SubjectUserSid

properties.displayName: Microsoft Defender protections disabled or excluded from the command line
properties.description:
Turning off real-time protection, adding broad exclusions, removing signatures or stopping the Defender services
clears the way for ransomware and tooling. Attackers usually do this minutes before the payload runs.
Seen in: BlackCat/ALPHV, LockBit, Black Basta and most other ransomware affiliates.
Tuning: software installers sometimes add narrow exclusions for their own folder; turn on Tamper Protection and manage
exclusions through Intune so command-line changes stand out.
Triage: check what was excluded or disabled, look for files dropped in that path, and restore protection. A Defender
change plus credential-dumping or shadow-copy activity on the same device means isolate now.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)set-mppreference.*-disable(realtimemonitoring|behaviormonitoring|ioavprotection|scriptscanning|blockatfirstseen|intrusionpreventionsystem|archivescanning)\s+(\$true|1)"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(add|set)-mppreference.*-exclusion(path|process|extension|ipaddress)"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)mpcmdrun(\.exe)?.*-removedefinitions"
    or (FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(stop|delete|config)\b.*\b(windefend|sense|wdboot|wdfilter|wdnissvc)\b")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: Device code sign-in by a user who doesn't normally use it
properties.description:
Device code phishing sends the victim a real Microsoft login code ("enter this code at microsoft.com/devicelogin to
join the meeting"). When they enter it, the attacker's device receives their tokens, MFA included. Most users never
use the device code flow, so a successful one from a user with no device-code history in 14 days deserves a look.
Seen in: Storm-2372 (2025) and other device code phishing campaigns aimed at Microsoft 365.
Tuning: conference-room devices, Azure CLI users and some IoT sign-ins use device code legitimately. The best fix is a
Conditional Access policy that blocks the device code flow for everyone who doesn't need it.
Triage: ask the user whether they entered a code. If not, revoke sessions, review sign-ins from the returned IPs and
check mailbox access (MailItemsAccessed) for the period after the sign-in.
properties.query:
let History = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. ago(1h))
    | where AuthenticationProtocol =~ "deviceCode"
    | distinct UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where AuthenticationProtocol =~ "deviceCode" and ResultType == "0"
| extend UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName)
| where UserPrincipalName !in (History)
| summarize FirstSignIn = min(TimeGenerated), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Locations = make_set(Location, 10),
    Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10)
    by UserPrincipalName

properties.displayName: Distributed password spray from many unfamiliar IPs
properties.description:
Low-and-slow sprays rotate through residential proxies so no single IP stands out, which defeats per-IP thresholds
(see the single-IP spray rule). This rule looks at the whole tenant: wrong-password failures from IPs that have had no
successful sign-in in 14 days, against 15+ users from 5+ IPs in an hour. It returns one row per source IP so each can
be blocked or investigated.
Seen in: Peach Sandstorm and Midnight Blizzard password spray campaigns.
Tuning: raise the thresholds for large tenants; check the first few runs against a normal hour's failure volume.
Triage: check whether any of these IPs also had a successful sign-in (search SigninLogs for ResultType 0 from them).
Users who were targeted and use weak or reused passwords should be reset first.
properties.query:
let minUsers = 15;
let minIPs = 5;
let KnownGoodIPs = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. ago(1h))
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | distinct IPAddress;
let Failures = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where ResultType == "50126"
    | where IPAddress !in (KnownGoodIPs);
let Campaign = Failures
    | summarize TargetedUsers = dcount(tolower(UserPrincipalName)), SourceIPCount = dcount(IPAddress)
    | where TargetedUsers >= minUsers and SourceIPCount >= minIPs;
Failures
| where toscalar(Campaign | count) > 0
| summarize Attempts = count(), Users = make_set(tolower(UserPrincipalName), 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Location = take_any(Location)
    by IPAddress
| extend CampaignUsers = toscalar(Campaign | project TargetedUsers), CampaignIPs = toscalar(Campaign | project SourceIPCount)

properties.displayName: Compliance search exported or used to purge mail
properties.description:
eDiscovery content search can export any mailbox in the organization or hard-delete matching messages everywhere.
Attackers with compliance roles use export to steal mail in bulk and purge to remove their phishing emails or alerts.
Tuning: legal and security teams run these; list their accounts and lower the severity for them rather than
excluding them, since their accounts are prime targets too.
Triage: check the search query and which mailboxes it covered (Get-ComplianceSearch), and confirm with legal or
security that the export or purge was requested.
properties.query:
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Operation =~ "New-ComplianceSearchAction"
| mv-apply P = todynamic(Parameters) on (
    summarize Params = make_bag(bag_pack(tostring(P.Name), tostring(P.Value)))
  )
| extend Action = case(isnotnull(Params.Purge), "Purge", isnotnull(Params.Export), "Export", "Other")
| where Action != "Other"
| project TimeGenerated, Actor = UserId, ClientIP, Action, SearchName = tostring(Params.SearchName),
    PurgeType = tostring(Params.PurgeType), Parameters

properties.displayName: PowerShell run with a long encoded command
properties.description:
-EncodedCommand (and its abbreviations, down to -e) takes base64 PowerShell, which hides the real script from casual
review and simple command-line rules. Long encoded commands from anything other than known management agents are
worth decoding. The Decoded column shows the script.
Seen in: Cobalt Strike, Empire and most PowerShell-based loaders.
Tuning: add your management agents (SCCM, Intune, RMM, backup) to ManagementParents after checking what they run.
Triage: read the Decoded column. Download cradles, AMSI bypasses or reflection mean isolate; vendor inventory scripts
mean add the parent to the allow-list.
properties.query:
let ManagementParents = dynamic(["ccmexec.exe", "senseir.exe", "microsoft.management.services.intunewindowsagent.exe", "agentexecutor.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "powershell_ise.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (ManagementParents)
| extend Encoded = extract(@"(?i)\s[-/]e(c|n|nc|nco|ncod|ncode|ncoded|ncodedc|ncodedco|ncodedcom|ncodedcomm|ncodedcomma|ncodedcomman|ncodedcommand)?\s+([A-Za-z0-9+/=]{100,})", 2, ProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(Encoded)
| extend Decoded = replace_regex(base64_decode_tostring(Encoded), @"\x00", "")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, Decoded, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: Entra Connect sync account used outside directory sync
properties.description:
The Entra Connect sync account (Sync_<server>_<id>@<tenant>.onmicrosoft.com) has broad directory rights and is
excluded from MFA in many tenants. It should only ever talk to the directory sync service. If it signs in to the
Azure portal, Graph Explorer, PowerShell or anything else, someone has taken its credentials from the sync server.
Seen in: Storm-0501 ransomware operations (2024), which moved from on-premises AD to Entra ID through the sync server.
Tuning: add the app name your sync account actually uses if it differs (check a week of its sign-ins first).
Triage: treat the sync server as compromised. Rotate the sync account password from the Entra Connect wizard, review
directory changes made by the account and check the server for credential theft.
properties.query:
let SyncApps = dynamic(["Microsoft Azure Active Directory Connect", "Microsoft Entra Connect", "Microsoft Online Syncfabric"]);
union
    (SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)),
    (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h))
| where UserPrincipalName startswith "sync_" and ResultType == "0"
| where AppDisplayName !in~ (SyncApps)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
    UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5) by UserPrincipalName

properties.displayName: Password spray against Entra ID from a single IP
properties.description:
Password spraying tries a few common passwords against many accounts to stay under lockout limits. The signal is one
source IP failing against many different users. A success from the same IP during the spray is the priority case.
Tuning: raise minUsers if you have shared egress IPs (VPN, proxies); exclude your own egress ranges.
Triage: Block the IP, check the SuccessCount users first (reset passwords, revoke sessions), and confirm MFA is enforced for
every targeted account.
properties.query:
let minUsers = 10;
let Window = SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h);
Window
| where ResultType in ("50126", "50053")
| summarize TargetedUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName), FailedAttempts = count(), SampleUsers = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 25),
    Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by IPAddress
| where TargetedUsers >= minUsers
| join kind=leftouter (
    Window | where ResultType == "0" | summarize SuccessfulUsers = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 25) by IPAddress
  ) on IPAddress
| extend SuccessCount = coalesce(array_length(SuccessfulUsers), 0)
| project IPAddress, TargetedUsers, FailedAttempts, SuccessCount, SuccessfulUsers, SampleUsers, Apps, FirstSeen, LastSeen

properties.displayName: Windows event log or audit policy cleared
properties.description:
Clearing the Security log (event 1102), clearing logs with wevtutil or PowerShell, or wiping audit policy removes
evidence of what just happened. It's a late-stage step, usually right before or after the damage.
Seen in: ransomware operators and APT intrusions (Volt Typhoon, BlackCat).
Tuning: lab and image-build machines sometimes clear logs; exclude them by device name.
Triage: treat the host as compromised. Logs already forwarded to Sentinel are intact; review the hour before the
clear for what was being hidden.
properties.query:
union
    (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where (FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s(cl|clear-log)\s")
        or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)clear-eventlog|remove-eventlog|globalsession\.clearlog|auditpol(\.exe)?\s+/(clear|remove)"
    | project TimeGenerated, HostName = DeviceName, Account = AccountName, Evidence = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents"),
    (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where EventID == 1102
    | project TimeGenerated, HostName = Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, Evidence = "Security log cleared (event 1102)", Source = "SecurityEvent")

properties.displayName: Domain federation settings changed in Entra ID
properties.description:
Changing a domain to federated, or changing its federation settings, lets whoever controls the identity provider
sign in as any user in that domain, MFA included. Attackers with Global Admin add their own IdP as a persistent
backdoor that survives password resets.
Seen in: Octo Tempest / Scattered Spider, and Golden SAML-style persistence after the SolarWinds intrusion.
Tuning: legitimate federation changes are rare and planned; match each alert to a change ticket.
Triage: check which domain changed, who did it and from where. If unplanned, revert the domain to managed
authentication, rotate the admin's credentials and review all Global Admin activity in the same session.
properties.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationName in ("Set domain authentication", "Set federation settings on domain") and Result =~ "success"
| extend Domain = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName),
    Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Domain, Actor, ActorIP

properties.displayName: Privileged Entra role assigned outside PIM
properties.description:
When privileged roles are managed through Privileged Identity Management (PIM), a direct, permanent assignment of
Global Administrator or a similar role bypasses approval and time limits. Attackers do this to keep access.
Tuning: PIM activations log a different operation ("Add member to role completed (PIM activation)") and are not
matched. Add any break-glass provisioning account to an allow list only after review.
Triage: Confirm the assignment with the actor. If unapproved, remove it, reset the target's credentials and review what the
role was used for.
properties.query:
let PrivilegedRoles = dynamic(["Global Administrator", "Privileged Role Administrator", "Privileged Authentication Administrator",
    "Security Administrator", "Exchange Administrator", "Application Administrator"]);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationName == "Add member to role" and Result =~ "success"
| mv-apply Prop = TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties on (
    where tostring(Prop.displayName) == "Role.DisplayName"
    | extend RoleName = trim(@'"', tostring(Prop.newValue))
  )
| where RoleName in (PrivilegedRoles)
| extend Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress), TargetUser = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| where Actor !startswith "MS-PIM"
| project TimeGenerated, RoleName, TargetUser, Actor, ActorIP

properties.displayName: Broad directory enumeration through Microsoft Graph
properties.description:
Tools like AzureHound, ROADrecon and GraphRunner pull users, groups, roles, apps, devices and policies in quick
succession to map paths to Global Admin. Normal apps read one or two kinds of directory object; this rule flags one
identity reading six or more kinds with 100+ requests in an hour.
Seen in: post-compromise reconnaissance by Midnight Blizzard, Storm-0501 and red teams using AzureHound.
Tuning: identity governance, backup and CSPM tools enumerate the directory by design; exclude their AppIds. Requires
the Microsoft Graph activity logs diagnostic setting.
Triage: identify the user or app and the user agent. An unknown user agent (python-requests, Go-http-client) from a
user account is the strongest sign; revoke the user's sessions and check how they signed in.
properties.query:
let DirectoryResources = dynamic(["users", "groups", "serviceprincipals", "applications", "directoryroles",
    "rolemanagement", "devices", "organization", "policies", "oauth2permissiongrants", "domains", "identity",
    "directoryobjects", "administrativeunits", "contacts", "groupsettings"]);
MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| extend Resource = tolower(extract(@"(?i)graph\.microsoft\.com/(?:v1\.0|beta)/([^/?]+)", 1, RequestUri))
| where Resource in (DirectoryResources)
| extend Identity = iff(isnotempty(UserId), UserId, ServicePrincipalId), IdentityType = iff(isnotempty(UserId), "User", "ServicePrincipal")
| summarize Requests = count(), ResourceTypes = dcount(Resource), Resources = make_set(Resource), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
    UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5), AppIds = make_set(AppId, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by Identity, IdentityType
| where ResourceTypes >= 6 and Requests >= 100

properties.displayName: Admin reset of password or MFA followed by sign-in from a new IP
properties.description:
Help-desk social engineering: the attacker calls IT pretending to be an employee, gets the password or MFA reset (or
a Temporary Access Pass issued), then signs in. This rule joins an admin-initiated password or security-info change
to a successful sign-in within two hours from an IP the user hasn't used in 14 days.
Seen in: Octo Tempest / Scattered Spider, and LAPSUS$-style intrusions.
Tuning: new hires and users locked out while traveling will appear; the IP and the help-desk ticket usually settle it.
Triage: find the ticket and call the user back on a number from HR records (not the one the caller gave). If the
user didn't ask for the reset, disable the account, revoke sessions and review everything it did since the reset.
properties.query:
let Resets = AuditLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(3h)
    | where OperationName in ("Reset password (by admin)", "Reset user password", "Admin registered security info",
        "Admin deleted security info", "Admin updated security info") and Result =~ "success"
    | extend UserPrincipalName = tolower(tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)),
        Admin = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName))
    | summarize ResetAt = min(TimeGenerated), Changes = make_set(OperationName), Admins = make_set(Admin) by UserPrincipalName;
let History = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. ago(3h))
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize KnownIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 500) by UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(3h)
| where ResultType == "0"
| extend UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName)
| join kind=inner Resets on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (ResetAt .. (ResetAt + 2h))
| join kind=leftouter History on UserPrincipalName
| extend KnownIPs = iff(isnull(KnownIPs), dynamic([]), KnownIPs)
| where not(set_has_element(KnownIPs, IPAddress))
| summarize FirstNewIPSignIn = min(TimeGenerated), NewIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Locations = make_set(Location, 10)
    by UserPrincipalName, ResetAt, Changes = tostring(Changes), Admin = tostring(Admins[0])

properties.displayName: Impacket-style remote execution (wmiexec, smbexec, DCOM)
properties.description:
Impacket's wmiexec and smbexec run commands on remote hosts and write the output to a file on the ADMIN$ or C$ share
(\\127.0.0.1\ADMIN$\__<timestamp>), which leaves a very recognizable command line. DCOM execution through MMC20 shows
up as mmc.exe -Embedding starting a shell.
Seen in: ransomware affiliates, Volt Typhoon and most red teams; Impacket is the standard lateral movement toolkit.
Tuning: no legitimate software writes output this way; expect zero false positives outside pentests.
Triage: identify the source host from DeviceLogonEvents (network logon just before), the account used, and contain
both ends. Reset the account's password.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/q\s+/c\s.*\\\\127\.0\.0\.1\\(admin|c)\$\\__")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mmc.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-Embedding" and FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe"))
| extend Method = case(InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "wmiprvse.exe", "wmiexec", InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "services.exe", "smbexec",
    InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mmc.exe", "dcomexec", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, Method, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: Inbox rule forwards mail to an external address
properties.description:
Attackers who take over a mailbox often add a rule that quietly forwards or redirects mail outside the company,
a key step in business email compromise.
Tuning: set OrgDomains to every domain you own. Expect occasional legitimate personal forwarding; confirm with the user
through a separate channel, not by email.
Triage: Remove the rule, check the sign-in that created it, revoke sessions and use message trace to see what was forwarded.
properties.query:
let OrgDomains = dynamic(["contoso.com"]);
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange" and Operation in~ ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule")
| mv-expand Param = todynamic(Parameters)
| where tostring(Param.Name) in~ ("ForwardTo", "ForwardAsAttachmentTo", "RedirectTo")
| mv-expand Destination = split(tostring(Param.Value), ";") to typeof(string)
| extend Destination = trim(@"\s", replace_regex(Destination, @"(?i)^smtp:", ""))
| extend DestinationDomain = tolower(tostring(split(Destination, "@")[1]))
| where isnotempty(DestinationDomain) and not(DestinationDomain in (OrgDomains))
| summarize Destinations = make_set(Destination), Operations = make_set(Operation) by TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP

properties.displayName: Inbox rule hides mail about payments or security
properties.description:
After taking over a mailbox, business email compromise (BEC) actors add a rule that deletes or buries replies about
invoices, wire transfers or "was this you?" security warnings, so the real owner doesn't notice the fraud in progress.
The rule names are often just "." or "..". This complements the external-forwarding rule, which covers rules that
send mail out.
Seen in: most BEC and AiTM follow-on activity documented by Microsoft and the FBI IC3.
Tuning: add finance or security words your users really use to the keyword list; rules that file vendor invoices into a
normal folder don't match because they don't hide mail.
Triage: look at the rule (Get-InboxRule -Mailbox <user>), check the sign-in that created it (ClientIP), and if it
isn't the user's, remove the rule, revoke sessions and find the messages the rule hid.
properties.query:
let Keywords = dynamic(["invoice", "invoices", "payment", "payments", "wire", "bank", "banking", "transfer", "remittance",
    "payroll", "deposit", "ach", "password", "phish", "phishing", "hack", "hacked", "compromised", "suspicious", "fraud",
    "mfa", "helpdesk", "verify", "unusual"]);
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Operation in~ ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule")
| mv-apply P = todynamic(Parameters) on (
    summarize Params = make_bag(bag_pack(tostring(P.Name), tostring(P.Value)))
  )
| extend RuleName = tostring(Params.Name), MoveTo = tostring(Params.MoveToFolder),
    Deletes = tostring(Params.DeleteMessage) =~ "True" or tostring(Params.SoftDeleteMessage) =~ "True",
    Words = tolower(strcat(tostring(Params.SubjectContainsWords), ";", tostring(Params.BodyContainsWords), ";",
        tostring(Params.SubjectOrBodyContainsWords), ";", tostring(Params.FromAddressContainsWords)))
| extend HidesMail = Deletes or MoveTo matches regex @"(?i)rss|archive|conversation history|junk|deleted items"
| extend KeywordMatch = Words has_any (Keywords), OddName = strlen(trim(@"[\s\.\,\-_']+", RuleName)) == 0
| where HidesMail and (KeywordMatch or OddName)
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, RuleName, MoveTo, Deletes, Words, Parameters

properties.displayName: Brute force against a device from a public IP (RDP, SMB or SSH)
properties.description:
Twenty or more failed logons to one device from one public IP in an hour means a management port is exposed to the
internet and being attacked. The Compromised column flags the cases where that same IP also logged on successfully.
Seen in: initial access for Dharma, Phobos and many other ransomware families through exposed RDP; SSH brute force
against Linux servers.
Tuning: none for the rule itself; fix the exposure (VPN, Bastion, just-in-time access) and the alerts stop.
Triage: if Compromised is true, isolate the device and investigate the session. Either way, close the port and check
the NSG rule (see the NSG management-port rule).
properties.query:
DeviceLogonEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Failures = countif(ActionType == "LogonFailed"), Successes = countif(ActionType == "LogonSuccess"),
    Accounts = make_set(AccountName, 20), SuccessAccounts = make_set_if(AccountName, ActionType == "LogonSuccess", 5),
    LogonTypes = make_set(LogonType), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| where Failures >= 20
| extend Compromised = Successes > 0

properties.displayName: Kerberoasting (many RC4 service tickets requested by one account)
properties.description:
Any domain user can request a service ticket for an account with an SPN, and the ticket is encrypted with that
account's password hash. Requesting RC4-encrypted tickets (type 0x17) for many SPNs at once and cracking them offline
is Kerberoasting. Service accounts with weak passwords fall in minutes.
Seen in: almost every Active Directory intrusion (Rubeus, Impacket GetUserSPNs).
Tuning: requires auditing of Kerberos Service Ticket Operations on domain controllers. Old applications that still
use RC4 request tickets for one or two SPNs; the five-SPN threshold skips them.
Triage: check the requesting account and source IP. Rotate the passwords of the requested service accounts (long
random passwords or gMSAs) and disable RC4 where possible.
properties.query:
let threshold = 5;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID == 4769 and TicketEncryptionType == "0x17"
| where ServiceName !endswith "$" and ServiceName !~ "krbtgt"
| summarize Services = dcount(ServiceName), ServiceList = make_set(ServiceName, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), DomainControllers = make_set(Computer, 5) by TargetUserName, IpAddress
| where Services >= threshold

properties.displayName: Mass secret retrieval from Azure Key Vault
properties.description:
One identity reading many distinct secrets, keys or certificates in a short window is a common sign of credential
harvesting after a compromise (or of a misconfigured script that needs fixing).
Tuning: start the threshold above your busiest legitimate automation; exclude known deployment identities by
appid. Requires Key Vault diagnostic logging (AuditEvent) sent to the workspace.
Triage: Rotate the secrets that were read, identify how the caller got access, and check where those secrets are used.
properties.query:
let threshold = 25;
AzureDiagnostics
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.KEYVAULT" and Category == "AuditEvent"
| where OperationName in ("SecretGet", "KeyGet", "CertificateGet")
| where ResultSignature == "OK"
| extend Caller = coalesce(identity_claim_upn_s, identity_claim_appid_g)
| summarize ItemsRead = dcount(id_s), Reads = count(), Vaults = make_set(Resource, 20),
    CallerIPs = make_set(CallerIPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Caller
| where ItemsRead >= threshold

properties.displayName: Successful sign-in over legacy authentication
properties.description:
Legacy protocols (IMAP, POP, SMTP AUTH, older Exchange protocols) can't do MFA, so password spraying and stolen
passwords work against them even when MFA is enforced elsewhere. A successful legacy sign-in means a password alone
got someone into the account.
Seen in: password spray campaigns that target IMAP and SMTP AUTH to get around MFA.
Tuning: scanners, printers and line-of-business apps that send mail over SMTP AUTH are the usual noise; move them to
OAuth or a connector and allow-list the accounts that remain. Blocking legacy auth with Conditional Access is the fix.
Triage: if the account isn't a known device or service account, treat it as compromised: reset the password, revoke
sessions and check the mailbox for rules and sent items.
properties.query:
let LegacyClients = dynamic(["IMAP4", "POP3", "Authenticated SMTP", "Exchange ActiveSync", "Exchange Web Services",
    "AutoDiscover", "MAPI Over HTTP", "Offline Address Book", "Outlook Anywhere (RPC over HTTP)",
    "Exchange Online PowerShell", "Other clients"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ResultType == "0" and ClientAppUsed in~ (LegacyClients)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), SignIns = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Locations = make_set(Location, 10)
    by UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName), ClientAppUsed

properties.displayName: Reverse shell command line on Linux
properties.description:
A reverse shell connects out from the compromised host to the attacker and hands them an interactive shell. The
one-liners are distinctive: bash's /dev/tcp, netcat with -e, socat exec:, a named pipe piped into nc, or a Python,
Perl, PHP or Ruby socket that duplicates file descriptors.
Seen in: exploitation of internet-facing Linux services (Confluence, Log4Shell, Ivanti), and cryptomining campaigns.
Tuning: penetration tests produce these; nothing else should.
Triage: get the destination IP and port, isolate the host, find the parent process (often a web server or Java
service, which points to the exploited application) and look for persistence such as cron jobs or SSH keys.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/dev/(tcp|udp)/[\w\.\-]+/\d+"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\b(nc|ncat|netcat|nc\.traditional)\b.*\s-(e|c)\s+\S*(sh|bash)\b"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"\bncat\b.*--(exec|sh-exec)\b"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bsocat\b.*\bexec:"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"mkfifo\s+\S+.*\|\s*(nc|ncat|netcat|/bin/(ba)?sh)\b"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"python[23]?(\.\d+)?\s+-c\s+.*socket.*(pty\.spawn|os\.dup2|subprocess)"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"perl\s+-e\s+.*socket.*exec"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"php\s+-r\s+.*fsockopen"
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"ruby\s+-rsocket"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: File downloaded with a built-in Windows tool
properties.description:
certutil, bitsadmin, mshta, regsvr32 and PowerShell's web cmdlets are signed Windows binaries that can fetch and run
remote payloads, so attackers use them instead of bringing their own downloader ("living off the land").
Seen in: initial-stage loaders and hands-on intrusions across the LOLBAS catalog.
Tuning: some software deployment scripts use bitsadmin or Invoke-WebRequest with -OutFile; allow-list them by parent
process or script path. PowerShell is only flagged when the download is executed (IEX) or saved as code.
Triage: get the URL, check what was downloaded and whether it ran (child processes, DeviceFileEvents), and block the
domain or IP.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where (FileName =~ "certutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)[-/](urlcache|verifyctl)\b" and ProcessCommandLine contains "http")
    or (FileName =~ "bitsadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/(transfer|addfile)\b")
    or (FileName =~ "mshta.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)https?://|javascript:|vbscript:")
    or (FileName =~ "regsvr32.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/i:\s*https?://|scrobj")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
        and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)downloadstring|downloadfile|downloaddata|invoke-webrequest|\biwr\b|invoke-restmethod|\birm\b|net\.webclient|start-bitstransfer"
        and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\biex\b|invoke-expression|-outfile\s+\S+\.(exe|dll|ps1|hta|bat|vbs|js)|\.(exe|dll|ps1|hta)['""\s]*\)?\s*$")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: LSASS memory dump by command line
properties.description:
Dumping the memory of lsass.exe gives an attacker every credential cached on the machine: NTLM hashes, Kerberos
tickets and sometimes clear-text passwords. Common methods are the comsvcs.dll MiniDump export through rundll32,
ProcDump with -ma against lsass, and tools such as Mimikatz, nanodump and lsassy.
Seen in: almost every hands-on-keyboard ransomware intrusion (The DFIR Report documents it repeatedly).
Tuning: support engineers occasionally dump lsass for Microsoft cases; those should be rare and ticketed. Turning on
the ASR rule "Block credential stealing from LSASS" and Credential Guard prevents most of these.
Triage: isolate the device, reset passwords for every account that signed in to it recently (privileged ones first),
and look for the dump file being copied off the machine.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where (FileName =~ "rundll32.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)comsvcs(\.dll)?[\s,]+(minidump|#\s*24)")
    or ((FileName in~ ("procdump.exe", "procdump64.exe") or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName in~ ("procdump", "procdump.exe"))
        and ProcessCommandLine has "lsass")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)sekurlsa::|out-minidump|nanodump|lsassy|pypykatz|mimikatz"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: Microsoft 365 audit logging turned off or bypassed
properties.description:
Turning off unified audit log ingestion, disabling mailbox auditing, or adding an audit bypass for an account blinds
every rule that reads OfficeActivity. Attackers do this before reading mail at scale.
Seen in: Midnight Blizzard and other actors targeting Microsoft 365 mail (Mandiant and CISA guidance on M365 logging).
Tuning: there should be no legitimate reason for these changes in production; investigate every one.
Triage: re-enable auditing immediately, identify the account and IP that made the change, and assume that account is
compromised until shown otherwise.
properties.query:
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Operation in~ ("Set-AdminAuditLogConfig", "Set-Mailbox", "Set-MailboxAuditBypassAssociation", "Set-OrganizationConfig")
| mv-apply P = todynamic(Parameters) on (
    summarize Params = make_bag(bag_pack(tostring(P.Name), tostring(P.Value)))
  )
| where (Operation =~ "Set-AdminAuditLogConfig" and (tostring(Params.UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled) =~ "False" or tostring(Params.AdminAuditLogEnabled) =~ "False"))
    or (Operation =~ "Set-Mailbox" and tostring(Params.AuditEnabled) =~ "False")
    or (Operation =~ "Set-MailboxAuditBypassAssociation" and tostring(Params.AuditBypassEnabled) =~ "True")
    or (Operation =~ "Set-OrganizationConfig" and tostring(Params.AuditDisabled) =~ "True")
| project TimeGenerated, Actor = UserId, ClientIP, Operation, Target = tostring(Params.Identity), Parameters

properties.displayName: Mailbox-level forwarding set to an external address
properties.description:
Set-Mailbox -ForwardingSmtpAddress copies every incoming message to another address. Unlike an inbox rule it doesn't
show in Outlook's rules list, so users rarely notice it. The inbox-rule forwarding rule doesn't see this.
Tuning: set OrgDomains to all of your accepted domains. Outbound spam policy can block automatic external forwarding
outright; if you've done that, this rule still shows the attempt.
Triage: confirm with the user and their manager. Remove the forward (Set-Mailbox -ForwardingSmtpAddress $null),
check who made the change and from where, and look at what was forwarded through message trace.
properties.query:
let OrgDomains = dynamic(["contoso.com"]);
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
