| where Operation =~ "Set-Mailbox"
| mv-apply P = todynamic(Parameters) on (
    summarize Params = make_bag(bag_pack(tostring(P.Name), tostring(P.Value)))
  )
| extend Mailbox = tostring(Params.Identity),
    ForwardTo = trim(@"\s", replace_regex(coalesce(tostring(Params.ForwardingSmtpAddress), tostring(Params.ForwardingAddress)), @"(?i)^smtp:", ""))
| extend ForwardDomain = tolower(tostring(split(ForwardTo, "@")[1]))
| where isnotempty(ForwardDomain) and not(ForwardDomain in (OrgDomains))
| project TimeGenerated, Actor = UserId, ClientIP, Mailbox, ForwardTo, ForwardDomain,
    KeepsCopy = tostring(Params.DeliverToMailboxAndForward)

properties.displayName: Full Access or Send As granted on a mailbox
properties.description:
FullAccess lets one account open another's mailbox; SendAs lets it send as them. Attackers with Exchange admin rights
grant themselves access to executives' or finance mailboxes for quiet collection and for payment fraud.
Tuning: assistants and shared mailboxes get these grants routinely; consider a watchlist of sensitive mailboxes
(executives, finance, legal) and alert only on those, or lower the severity for everything else.
Triage: confirm the grant with the mailbox owner. Remove it if unexpected, and check MailItemsAccessed for the grantee.
properties.query:
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Operation in~ ("Add-MailboxPermission", "Add-RecipientPermission")
| where UserId !startswith "NT AUTHORITY"
| mv-apply P = todynamic(Parameters) on (
    summarize Params = make_bag(bag_pack(tostring(P.Name), tostring(P.Value)))
  )
| extend Mailbox = tostring(Params.Identity), Grantee = coalesce(tostring(Params.User), tostring(Params.Trustee)),
    AccessRights = tostring(Params.AccessRights)
| where AccessRights has_any ("FullAccess", "SendAs")
| project TimeGenerated, Actor = UserId, ClientIP, Operation, Mailbox, Grantee, AccessRights

properties.displayName: Mass deletion of users, groups or apps in Entra ID
properties.description:
Ten or more user, group or application deletions by one account in an hour. Destructive attackers (and departing
insiders) delete accounts to lock the organization out or slow the response.
Tuning: offboarding scripts and HR-driven deprovisioning run in bulk; exclude their service principals by name.
Triage: confirm with the actor. If unexpected, disable the actor, then restore the deleted objects from the Entra
recycle bin (they're recoverable for 30 days).
properties.query:
let threshold = 10;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationName in ("Delete user", "Delete group", "Delete application", "Hard delete user") and Result =~ "success"
| extend Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    Target = coalesce(tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName), tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName))
| summarize Deletions = count(), Operations = make_set(OperationName), Targets = make_set(Target, 50),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Actor
| where Deletions >= threshold

properties.displayName: Mass file download from SharePoint or OneDrive
properties.description:
A single account downloading hundreds of distinct files in an hour can mean data theft by an attacker or a departing
employee.
Tuning: set the threshold above normal sync behavior for your users; exclude backup and migration service accounts.
Pair with your offboarding list for insider-risk cases.
Triage: Check the device and IP used, ask the user (and their manager) about the downloads, and revoke sessions if the
activity isn't theirs.
properties.query:
let threshold = 200;
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OfficeWorkload in ("SharePoint", "OneDrive") and Operation in ("FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| summarize FilesDownloaded = dcount(SourceFileName), Sites = make_set(Site_Url, 10), ClientIPs = make_set(ClientIP, 10),
    FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserId
| where FilesDownloaded >= threshold

properties.displayName: New MFA method followed by sign-in from a new country
properties.description:
After stealing a password and session, attackers register their own MFA method so they can come back. A new security
method followed within an hour by a successful sign-in from a country the user has not signed in from in two weeks is
a strong account-takeover signal.
Tuning: travelers will trigger this occasionally; the registration plus the new country together keep volume low.
Triage: Remove the new MFA method, revoke sessions, reset the password, and look for inbox rules or app consents added in
the same session.
properties.query:
let Registrations = AuditLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
    | where OperationName in ("User registered security info", "User changed default security info") and Result =~ "success"
    | extend UserPrincipalName = tolower(tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName))
    | project UserPrincipalName, RegisteredAt = TimeGenerated, Registration = OperationName;
let History = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. ago(2h))
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize KnownCountries = make_set(Location) by UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where ResultType == "0"
| extend UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName)
| join kind=inner Registrations on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (RegisteredAt .. (RegisteredAt + 1h))
| join kind=leftouter History on UserPrincipalName
| extend KnownCountries = iff(isnull(KnownCountries), dynamic([]), KnownCountries)
| where not(set_has_element(KnownCountries, Location))
| summarize FirstSignIn = min(TimeGenerated), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10)
    by UserPrincipalName, Location, RegisteredAt, Registration, KnownCountries = tostring(KnownCountries)

properties.displayName: Conditional Access named location added, changed or deleted
properties.description:
Named locations feed Conditional Access. Marking an attacker-controlled IP range as trusted can skip MFA or
location blocks without touching any policy, so the existing CA-policy rule never fires.
Tuning: network teams update named locations when offices or VPN egress change; tie each change to a ticket.
The IsTrusted column shows whether the new definition marks the range as trusted.
Triage: check the IP ranges in NewValue against your known office, VPN and cloud egress ranges.
properties.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationName in ("Add named location", "Update named location", "Delete named location") and Result =~ "success"
| extend Location = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName),
    NewValue = tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties[0].newValue),
    Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| extend IsTrusted = NewValue contains '"isTrusted":true'
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Location, IsTrusted, NewValue, Actor, ActorIP

properties.displayName: Network security group rule opens RDP, SSH or WinRM to the internet
properties.description:
An inbound allow rule from any source to 3389, 22, 5985 or 5986 exposes the VM to constant brute forcing within
minutes. Attackers open these ports for direct access; admins open them "temporarily" and forget.
Tuning: if you use Azure Bastion or just-in-time VM access, legitimate rules shouldn't use * or Internet as the
source. Port ranges (for example 3380-3390) aren't parsed; the explicit ports and * are.
Triage: remove or narrow the rule, then check DeviceLogonEvents or SecurityEvent on the VM for logons from public IPs
while it was open.
properties.query:
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationNameValue in~ ("MICROSOFT.NETWORK/NETWORKSECURITYGROUPS/SECURITYRULES/WRITE", "MICROSOFT.NETWORK/NETWORKSECURITYGROUPS/WRITE")
| where ActivityStatusValue !in~ ("Failure", "Failed")
| extend Body = parse_json(tostring(Properties_d.requestbody))
| mv-expand Rule = iff(isnotnull(Body.properties.securityRules), Body.properties.securityRules, pack_array(Body))
| extend R = Rule.properties
| extend Source = strcat(tostring(R.sourceAddressPrefix), ",", strcat_array(R.sourceAddressPrefixes, ",")),
    Ports = strcat(tostring(R.destinationPortRange), ",", strcat_array(R.destinationPortRanges, ","))
| where tostring(R.access) =~ "Allow" and tostring(R.direction) =~ "Inbound"
| where Source matches regex @"(?i)(^|,)\s*(\*|0\.0\.0\.0/0|internet|any)\s*(,|$)"
| where Ports matches regex @"(^|,)\s*(\*|22|3389|5985|5986)\s*(,|$)"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by Caller, CallerIpAddress, RuleId = _ResourceId, RuleName = tostring(Rule.name), Source, Ports

properties.displayName: Active Directory database (NTDS.dit) extraction
properties.description:
NTDS.dit holds the password hash of every account in the domain. Attackers copy it from a domain controller with
ntdsutil "ifm", or from a volume shadow copy, then crack or pass the hashes offline. Finding this means the whole
domain's credentials should be treated as stolen.
Seen in: Volt Typhoon, and ransomware intrusions documented by CISA and The DFIR Report.
Tuning: AD backup products don't use these commands; expect close to zero legitimate hits.
Triage: confirm on the DC, find where the copy went, and start a domain-wide credential reset plan (krbtgt twice,
privileged accounts, service accounts).
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where (FileName =~ "ntdsutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bifm\b")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\ntds\.dit"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: Consent granted to an app with high-risk permissions
properties.description:
Consent phishing tricks a user or admin into granting an app broad access (mail, files, directory). The app then reads
data without needing a password or MFA.
Tuning: adjust HighRiskScopes to your policy. Known business apps can be excluded by AppId after review; better still,
restrict user consent in Entra ID so this rule mostly fires on admin consent.
Triage: Review the app's publisher and permissions. If suspicious, revoke the grant, disable the service principal and check
what it accessed (Graph activity logs, MailItemsAccessed).
properties.query:
let HighRiskScopes = dynamic(["Mail.Read", "Mail.ReadWrite", "Mail.Send", "MailboxSettings.ReadWrite",
    "Files.ReadWrite.All", "Sites.ReadWrite.All", "Directory.ReadWrite.All", "User.ReadWrite.All",
    "Application.ReadWrite.All", "RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory", "full_access_as_app"]);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationName == "Consent to application" and Result =~ "success"
| mv-apply Prop = TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties on (
    where tostring(Prop.displayName) == "ConsentAction.Permissions"
    | extend Permissions = tostring(Prop.newValue)
  )
| extend RiskyScopes = set_intersect(HighRiskScopes, extract_all(@"([\w\.]+)", Permissions))
| where array_length(RiskyScopes) > 0
| extend AppName = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName), AppId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id),
    ConsentedBy = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), ConsentIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| project TimeGenerated, AppName, AppId, ConsentedBy, ConsentIP, RiskyScopes

properties.displayName: Office application launches a shell, script host or LOLBin
properties.description:
Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook or OneNote starting PowerShell, cmd, mshta, rundll32 or similar is the classic sign of
a malicious document or attachment running its first stage.
Seen in: Emotet, Qakbot, IcedID and countless phishing loaders; blocked by the ASR rule "Block all Office applications
from creating child processes".
Tuning: some Excel add-ins and mail-merge tools start cmd.exe; check the command line and allow-list the specific
add-in path if needed. Turning on the ASR rule in block mode is the real fix.
Triage: get the document (from the email or the device), check what the child process did next (network connections,
dropped files), and isolate the device if anything ran.

properties.displayName: Account suddenly emails far more recipients than usual
properties.description:
A compromised mailbox is often used straight away to phish colleagues, customers and suppliers, because mail from a
real account passes every reputation check. This rule flags a sender who reached 100+ recipients in the last hour and
more than three times their busiest hour in the previous two weeks.
Tuning: marketing and communications senders have high baselines and won't fire unless they spike further; brand-new
mailboxes have no baseline and will fire if they hit the threshold.
Triage: read a sample of the messages (subject, links). If it's phishing, block the sender, revoke sessions, reset
the password and purge the messages; then warn external recipients.
properties.query:
let minRecipients = 100;
let Baseline = EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. ago(1h))
    | where EmailDirection in~ ("Outbound", "Intra-org")
    | summarize Recipients = dcount(RecipientEmailAddress) by Sender = tolower(SenderFromAddress), Hour = bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
    | summarize BaselineMaxPerHour = max(Recipients) by Sender;
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EmailDirection in~ ("Outbound", "Intra-org")
| summarize Recipients = dcount(RecipientEmailAddress), Messages = count(), WithUrls = countif(UrlCount > 0),
    Subjects = make_set(Subject, 5) by Sender = tolower(SenderFromAddress)
| join kind=leftouter Baseline on Sender
| extend BaselineMaxPerHour = iff(isnull(BaselineMaxPerHour), 0, BaselineMaxPerHour)
| where Recipients >= minRecipients and Recipients > 3 * BaselineMaxPerHour
| project Sender, Recipients, Messages, WithUrls, BaselineMaxPerHour, Subjects

properties.displayName: Per-user MFA disabled for an account
properties.description:
Turning off per-user MFA lets the account sign in with a password alone wherever Conditional Access doesn't step in.
Attackers with admin rights do this to keep access to accounts they control.
Tuning: if you've moved fully to Conditional Access and are retiring per-user MFA, these changes are expected during
the migration; scope the alert to after the migration date.
Triage: confirm the change with the admin and the user. Re-enable MFA or confirm a Conditional Access policy covers the
account.
properties.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where OperationName == "Disable Strong Authentication" and Result =~ "success"
| extend TargetUser = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName),
    Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| project TimeGenerated, TargetUser, Actor, ActorIP

properties.displayName: User clicked a link in a delivered phishing email
properties.description:
Defender for Office 365 classified the email as phishing but it still reached the inbox (policy gap, allow-list,
or a verdict that came after delivery), and the user clicked through. This is the moment to act, before the
credentials or session are used.
Tuning: requires Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 (EmailEvents and UrlClickEvents). Clicks blocked by Safe Links are
left out because they didn't reach the page.
Triage: reset the user's password and revoke sessions if the URL was a credential page; check sign-ins in the next
hour for a new IP or a new MFA method (see the AiTM and MFA-registration rules). Purge the email from all mailboxes.
properties.query:
let Phish = EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ThreatTypes has "Phish" and DeliveryAction =~ "Delivered"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress = tolower(RecipientEmailAddress), SenderFromAddress, Subject, DeliveryLocation;
UrlClickEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ActionType =~ "ClickAllowed" or IsClickedThrough == true
| extend AccountUpn = tolower(AccountUpn)
| join kind=inner Phish on NetworkMessageId, $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| summarize FirstClick = min(TimeGenerated), Urls = make_set(Url, 10), ClickIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 5)
    by AccountUpn, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, Subject

properties.displayName: Member added to a privileged Active Directory group
properties.description:
Adding an account to Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Administrators or another built-in privileged group is the
usual way attackers make their access stick on-premises. These groups should change rarely, and through a process.
Tuning: if you use a privileged access management tool that adds members temporarily, exclude its service account
(SubjectUserName).
Triage: confirm with the person who made the change (SubjectUserName). If unapproved, remove the member, reset its
password, and review what the account did while privileged.
properties.query:
let PrivilegedGroups = dynamic(["Domain Admins", "Enterprise Admins", "Schema Admins", "Administrators", "Account Operators",
    "Backup Operators", "Server Operators", "Print Operators", "DnsAdmins", "Group Policy Creator Owners", "Enterprise Key Admins",
    "Key Admins", "Exchange Windows Permissions", "Organization Management"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID in (4728, 4732, 4756)
| where TargetUserName in~ (PrivilegedGroups)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Group = TargetUserName, Member = MemberName, AddedBy = SubjectUserName, EventID

properties.displayName: Mass file renaming to a new extension (possible ransomware encryption)
properties.description:
Most ransomware renames each file it encrypts with its own extension. One process renaming 100+ files to the same
unusual extension within 15 minutes is the encryption itself, and every minute counts.
Tuning: common document, image, archive and temp extensions are excluded so Office saves, sync clients and backup
tools don't fire. Add extensions your own tools produce.
Triage: isolate the device immediately (and any server whose shares it's writing to), identify the process and how
it started, and check whether other devices show the same extension.
properties.query:
let threshold = 100;
let CommonExtensions = dynamic(["doc", "docx", "xls", "xlsx", "ppt", "pptx", "pdf", "txt", "csv", "jpg", "jpeg", "png", "gif",
    "zip", "7z", "rar", "tmp", "temp", "log", "bak", "old", "partial", "crdownload", "part", "json", "xml", "dat", "db", "msg", "eml"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(15m)
| where ActionType == "FileRenamed"
| extend NewExt = tolower(extract(@"\.([^.\\/]+)$", 1, FileName)), OldExt = tolower(extract(@"\.([^.\\/]+)$", 1, PreviousFileName))
| where isnotempty(NewExt) and NewExt != OldExt and NewExt !in (CommonExtensions)
| summarize Renamed = count(), SampleFiles = make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
    AccountName = take_any(InitiatingProcessAccountName)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, NewExt
| where Renamed >= threshold

properties.displayName: SAM, SECURITY or SYSTEM registry hive saved to disk
properties.description:
Saving the SAM, SECURITY and SYSTEM hives with reg.exe lets an attacker extract local account hashes, cached domain
credentials and LSA secrets (including service account passwords) offline.
Seen in: ransomware precursors and the Volt Typhoon and Scattered Spider playbooks.
Tuning: legitimate backups use VSS, not reg save, so this should almost never fire for real admin work.
Triage: find where the files were written and whether they left the device; reset the local administrator password
(LAPS) and any service account whose secret lives in LSA on that host.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where (FileName =~ "reg.exe" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "reg.exe")
    and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(save|export)\b.*\b(hklm|hkey_local_machine)\\(sam|security|system)(\s|""|$)"
    or (FileName =~ "esentutl.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\config\\(sam|security|system)\b")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: Email with a high-risk attachment type delivered to the inbox
properties.description:
Disk images (ISO, IMG, VHD), shortcuts (LNK), scripts, OneNote files, SVG images and other formats that run code or
carry HTML smuggling are favorite loaders because they slip past older attachment filters. Few businesses need to
receive them by email.
Seen in: Qakbot, IcedID, Emotet and recent SVG-based credential phishing waves.
Tuning: if a supplier legitimately sends one of these types, allow-list that sender domain. Better still, add these
extensions to the anti-malware common attachments filter and keep this rule as a check that the filter works.
Triage: detonate or look up the hash, check whether the recipient opened it (DeviceFileEvents for the file name on
their device), and purge the message from all mailboxes.
properties.query:
let RiskyExtensions = dynamic(["iso", "img", "vhd", "vhdx", "lnk", "hta", "js", "jse", "vbs", "vbe", "wsf", "wsh", "one",
    "chm", "scr", "cpl", "svg", "xll", "msc", "appx", "msix", "library-ms", "pif", "jar", "ps1", "bat", "cmd"]);
EmailAttachmentInfo
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| extend Extension = tolower(extract(@"\.([A-Za-z0-9\-]+)$", 1, FileName))
| where Extension in (RiskyExtensions) or tolower(FileType) in (RiskyExtensions)
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where EmailDirection =~ "Inbound" and DeliveryAction =~ "Delivered" and DeliveryLocation !in~ ("Quarantine", "Junk folder")
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, SenderFromDomain, DeliveryLocation
  ) on NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress
| summarize Recipients = make_set(RecipientEmailAddress, 50), RecipientCount = dcount(RecipientEmailAddress), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
    by FileName, Extension, SHA256, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, Subject
| extend HashAlgorithm = "SHA256"

properties.displayName: High-risk sign-in succeeded with a password only
properties.description:
Entra ID Protection rated the sign-in high risk (for example an anonymizing IP, a password known to be leaked, or an
unfamiliar location with attacker-like properties), yet it succeeded without MFA. Either a risk-based Conditional
Access policy is missing or this user is excluded from it.
Tuning: requires Entra ID P2. If this fires often, the fix is a sign-in risk policy that requires MFA, not a filter.
Triage: confirm the sign-in with the user, check the risk detail in Entra ID Protection, and if unexplained, reset the
password and revoke sessions. Then find out why MFA wasn't required.
properties.query:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ResultType == "0" and RiskLevelDuringSignIn =~ "high" and AuthenticationRequirement =~ "singleFactorAuthentication"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, ConditionalAccessStatus

properties.displayName: Remote access (RMM) tool runs on a device for the first time
properties.description:
Attackers install legitimate remote-management tools (AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, Atera, Splashtop, NetSupport,
RustDesk and others) because they're signed, trusted by antivirus and blend in with IT. A tool that hasn't run on
this device in 14 days and isn't your approved one deserves a question.
Seen in: Scattered Spider, Black Basta (Teams vishing followed by Quick Assist/AnyDesk), and CISA advisory AA23-025A on
RMM abuse.
Tuning: put your sanctioned tool's executable names in ApprovedTools. Block the rest with WDAC or AppLocker.
Triage: ask the user whether IT or a "support" caller had them install it. Uninstall, check the tool's logs for
incoming sessions, and review what happened on the device during those sessions.
properties.query:
let ApprovedTools = dynamic(["approved-rmm-agent.exe"]);
let RmmPattern = @"(?i)^(anydesk|screenconnect\..*|connectwisecontrol\..*|atera.*agent|splashtop.*|srservice|teamviewer.*|tv_[wx]64|netsupport.*|client32|rustdesk|meshagent|tacticalrmm|rutserv|rfusclient|supremo.*|zohoassist.*|dwagent|simplehelp.*|remotepc.*|getscreen|ammyy.*|action1_agent|quickassist)\.exe$";
let Known = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. ago(1h))
    | where FileName matches regex RmmPattern
    | distinct DeviceName, Tool = tolower(FileName);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where FileName matches regex RmmPattern
| extend Tool = tolower(FileName)
| where Tool !in (ApprovedTools)
| join kind=leftanti Known on DeviceName, Tool
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), AccountName = take_any(AccountName), FolderPath = take_any(FolderPath),
    Parents = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5), CommandLines = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 5) by DeviceName, Tool

properties.displayName: Run key or Winlogon value points to a script host or user-writable folder
properties.description:
Run and RunOnce keys (and the Winlogon Shell and Userinit values) start programs at every logon. Malware writes its
loader path there, typically in AppData, Temp or Public, or as a PowerShell or mshta one-liner.
Seen in: commodity malware, infostealers and RATs (AsyncRAT, Remcos, njRAT) as well as hands-on intrusions.
Tuning: well-known apps that install per-user (OneDrive, Teams, Slack, Discord, Zoom) are excluded; add others you
allow after checking them.
Triage: check the file the value points to (hash, signer, prevalence), delete the value, and find what wrote it.
properties.query:
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey matches regex @"(?i)\\software\\(wow6432node\\)?microsoft\\windows\\currentversion\\(run|runonce|runonceex|policies\\explorer\\run)$"
    or (RegistryKey matches regex @"(?i)\\microsoft\\windows nt\\currentversion\\winlogon$" and RegistryValueName in~ ("Userinit", "Shell"))
| where RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)\\(appdata|temp|users\\public|programdata|perflogs)\\|powershell|pwsh|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|wscript|cscript|cmd(\.exe)?\s+/c|https?://"
| where not(RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)\\appdata\\local\\(microsoft\\(onedrive|teams)|slack|discord|zoom)\\")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName

properties.displayName: Service principal signs in from a new country
properties.description:
Apps and service principals usually sign in from a fixed set of places (your cloud regions, your CI runners). A
successful sign-in from a country the service principal hasn't used in 14 days often means its secret or certificate
was stolen and is being used elsewhere.
Seen in: Midnight Blizzard and Storm-0558 follow-on activity, and leaked client secrets in public repositories.
Tuning: only service principals with sign-in history are checked, so brand-new apps don't alert. Multi-region
workloads may need their extra countries added.
Triage: check which credential was used (Entra sign-in details show the key ID), rotate it, and review what the
service principal accessed (Graph activity logs, Azure activity).
properties.query:
let Known = AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. ago(1h))
    | where ResultType == "0" and isnotempty(Location)
    | summarize KnownCountries = make_set(Location, 100) by ServicePrincipalId;
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ResultType == "0" and isnotempty(Location)
| join kind=inner Known on ServicePrincipalId
| where not(set_has_element(KnownCountries, Location))
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), SignIns = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10)
    by ServicePrincipalName, ServicePrincipalId, AppId, Location, KnownCountries = tostring(KnownCountries)

properties.displayName: Shadow copy or backup catalog deletion
properties.description:
Ransomware deletes Volume Shadow Copies and backup catalogs, and turns off Windows recovery, so victims can't restore
files. These commands are rare in normal operations and usually come minutes before encryption starts.
Tuning: allow-list documented backup software only after confirming its command lines. Treat any hit as a possible
active incident.
Triage: Isolate the device now: shadow copy deletion is usually seconds before encryption. Then look for the same commands on
other hosts.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(15m)
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete", "shadows"))
    or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy", "delete"))
    or (FileName =~ "wbadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete", "catalog"))
    or (FileName =~ "bcdedit.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "recoveryenabled" and ProcessCommandLine has "no")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Win32_ShadowCopy"
        and (ProcessCommandLine contains "Delete" or ProcessCommandLine contains "Remove-"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: Scheduled task created that runs a script host, LOLBin or file from a user-writable folder
properties.description:
Scheduled tasks are the most common persistence method on Windows. Tasks created from the command line that run
hidden PowerShell, mshta, rundll32 or a binary in AppData, Temp or Public are rarely legitimate.
Seen in: Qakbot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike operators and most commodity malware.
Tuning: some per-user updaters (browsers, chat apps) run from AppData; allow-list them by task name.
Triage: read the /tr command, delete the task (schtasks /delete /tn <name> /f), check whether it already ran, and
find the process that created it.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s/create\s"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/tr\s+.*(powershell.*\s-(e|ec|enc|encodedcommand|w\s+hidden|windowstyle\s+hidden)\b|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|wscript|cscript|certutil|bitsadmin|https?://|\\(appdata|temp|users\\public|programdata|perflogs)\\)"
| extend TaskName = extract(@"(?i)/tn\s+(""[^""]+""|\S+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, TaskName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: Service created that runs a shell, script or binary from a user-writable folder
properties.description:
Services run as SYSTEM and start at boot, so attackers create them for persistence and to execute payloads on
remote hosts (sc \\host create ...). Real software installs services from Program Files, not from Temp or Public, and
not as "cmd /c powershell ...".
Seen in: Cobalt Strike's service-based lateral movement, PsExec-style tooling and many ransomware deployments.
Tuning: a few in-house tools might install from ProgramData; allow-list their exact binPath.
Triage: get the binPath, check whether the service ran and what it started, delete it, and look for the same service
name on other hosts.
properties.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\screate\s"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)binpath=\s*.*(cmd(\.exe)?\s+/c|powershell|pwsh|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|%comspec%|\\(appdata|temp|users\\public|programdata|perflogs)\\|\\\\127\.0\.0\.1\\)"
| extend RemoteTarget = extract(@"(?i)sc(\.exe)?\s+(\\\\[^\s]+)\s+create", 2, ProcessCommandLine)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, RemoteTarget, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

properties.displayName: Exchange transport rule copies, redirects or deletes mail
properties.description:
Transport (mail flow) rules apply to the whole organization. A rule that BCCs, redirects or silently deletes messages
lets an attacker with Exchange admin rights read or hide mail for everyone, and it survives password resets.
Tuning: legal journaling and compliance copies are the usual legitimate uses; they're set up rarely and on purpose.
Triage: review the rule (Get-TransportRule), who created it and from which IP. Disable it first if the destination is
outside the company, then investigate.
properties.query:
let RiskyActions = dynamic(["BlindCopyTo", "RedirectMessageTo", "AddToRecipients", "CopyTo", "DeleteMessage",
    "RouteMessageOutboundConnector", "ModerateMessageByUser"]);
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Operation in~ ("New-TransportRule", "Set-TransportRule")
| mv-apply P = todynamic(Parameters) on (
    summarize Params = make_bag(bag_pack(tostring(P.Name), tostring(P.Value)))
  )
| extend Actions = set_intersect(bag_keys(Params), RiskyActions),
    BypassesSpam = tostring(Params.SetSCL) == "-1"
| where array_length(Actions) > 0 or BypassesSpam
| project TimeGenerated, Actor = UserId, ClientIP, Operation, RuleName = tostring(Params.Name), Actions, BypassesSpam, Parameters

properties.displayName: Web server process starts a shell or reconnaissance command (possible web shell)
properties.description:
IIS worker processes, Exchange's UM worker, Apache, nginx, PHP and Tomcat shouldn't start cmd, PowerShell, sh or
whoami. When they do, someone is usually running commands through a web shell planted via an exploited
vulnerability.
Seen in: ProxyLogon/ProxyShell exploitation of Exchange, MOVEit and other edge-application exploits, Hafnium and Volt
Typhoon.
Tuning: some legacy web apps shell out by design; allow-list the exact command line, not the parent.
Triage: find the web shell (recently written .aspx, .jsp or .php files in web roots), check the web logs for the
requests that triggered it, and patch the exploited application.
